client: I've been really struggling since starting this new marketing job. The deadlines feel impossible to meet, and I keep comparing myself to my coworkers who seem to know exactly what they're doing. Part of me wonders if talking about it will help, since the pressure isn't going away.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy load of self-doubt while adjusting to this new role, and that comparison with your coworkers is adding extra pressure. I'm curious—when you notice those thoughts about others seeming to know exactly what they're doing, what specific qualities or actions are you comparing yourself to?

client: I keep noticing how quickly some of my coworkers speak up in meetings with perfect answers, while I'm still processing the information. It makes me feel like I'm always two steps behind, even though I know logically that I'm still learning. The worst part is when I do finally think of something to contribute, I second-guess myself and stay quiet.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you'd feel frustrated when your natural processing style differs from others', especially when it leads to self-doubt about your valuable contributions. I wonder if we could explore what might happen if you viewed this thoughtful processing time as a strength rather than a weakness?

client: I get what you're saying about reframing it as a strength, but it's hard when everyone else at work seems to make decisions so quickly. I always feel like I'm slowing things down, and that makes me anxious about speaking up. Even if I do have good ideas later, by then the moment has usually passed.
therapist: That anxiety about "missing the moment" sounds really painful, and I hear how it's creating a cycle where you hesitate and then feel even more pressure. What would it be like to experiment with sharing just one thought in a meeting, even if it feels slightly delayed—how do you imagine that might go?

client:
I get what you're saying, but the idea of speaking up even a little late makes me panic. What if people think I'm slow or not paying attention? I already feel like I'm always a step behind in conversations, and forcing it might just make me look worse. 

It's not just about the timing - when I do speak, my mind goes blank and I worry my contribution won't be valuable enough. The pressure to say something perfect makes me freeze up completely.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming this feels—like you're caught between wanting to contribute and fearing that whatever you say won't measure up. It might help to explore what "valuable enough" looks like to you—what would a genuinely imperfect but acceptable contribution sound like in your mind?

client: I don't know, when I try to imagine what "good enough" would look like, my mind just goes blank. It's like there's this invisible standard I can't even see, but I know I'm failing it. When people at work ask for my input in meetings, my throat closes up because what if what I say is stupid or obvious?
therapist: It sounds like that "invisible standard" feels impossible to meet, and the fear of being judged is so intense that it’s physically stopping you from speaking. What do you think might happen if you started by practicing sharing smaller, less "perfect" thoughts with someone you trust outside of work?

client: I get what you're saying, but even with people I trust, I freeze up. What if they think my "small thoughts" are stupid or pointless? The idea of sharing anything imperfect makes my chest tighten up. It's like my brain screams that anything less than profound insight isn't worth saying.
therapist: That inner critic sounds incredibly harsh—it's as if your mind has decided that only profound insights deserve to be heard, which must feel exhausting to live with. I wonder if we could gently explore where that belief comes from—when did you first start feeling that your thoughts needed to meet such a high standard to be valuable?

client: I think it started back in college when I had this professor who always dismissed my ideas unless they were "groundbreaking." Now I feel like if my thoughts aren't deep or unique, they're not worth sharing. But honestly, I'm not sure digging into the past will help—it just feels like making excuses for why I'm like this now.
therapist: It makes sense that this professor's criticism left a deep mark, and I hear your reluctance to dwell on the past—this isn't about excuses, but about understanding how that experience shaped the impossible standards you hold yourself to now. What would it feel like to challenge that professor's definition of "valuable" by considering that most everyday contributions—even simple questions or observations—keep teams moving forward?

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's hard to shake the feeling that if even my professor—someone who's supposed to mentor students—thought my contributions weren't good enough, then maybe they really weren't. I keep replaying that moment where he sighed and moved on from my question in class like it was wasting everyone's time. 

The idea of challenging his definition feels... almost disrespectful somehow? Like I'd just be making excuses for not being smart enough.
therapist: It sounds like that moment with your professor carried a deep sense of rejection, and now questioning his judgment feels like questioning reality itself—as if his sigh confirmed something fundamental about your worth. I wonder if we could sit with this gently: what if respecting yourself meant acknowledging that even mentors can be wrong, and that their reactions sometimes say more about them than about you?

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's hard to shake the feeling that he's right. He's been teaching for decades, so if he sighed at my work, doesn't that mean it really wasn't good enough? I keep replaying that moment in my head and it makes my stomach twist up. 

The idea that his reaction might be about him and not me... I want to believe that, but it feels like making excuses for myself. Like I'm just trying to avoid facing the truth that I'm not cut out for this program.
therapist: It's clear how much this moment still affects you, and how that sigh became proof of something painful about your abilities—that must feel so heavy to carry. I wonder if we could explore what might shift if you considered that even experienced teachers can have off days, or that one person's sigh doesn't define the value of your thoughts?

client:
I get what you're saying, but it's hard to believe that sigh didn't mean something. I keep replaying that moment in my head - the way my professor sighed and looked away when I asked a question after class. It just confirmed all my fears that my ideas aren't good enough. 

Even if it was just an off day for her, it still makes me not want to speak up in class anymore. What if I embarrass myself again?
therapist: That moment clearly became a turning point where her reaction reinforced your deepest fears about not measuring up—no wonder it still feels so raw. What would it be like to acknowledge how much that hurt while also gently questioning whether one moment should have the power to silence all your future contributions?
